Train an automated scorer on human-scored text

Source: R/ai-scoring.R
train_scorer.Rd

Fits a simple, transparent automated scoring engine: A ridge regression of human scores on the words of the responses ("bag of words"). It runs in base R with no internet connection and no API key, so it suits teaching and small programs, and it plugs straight into score_open() through its predict() method.

Usage

train_scorer(
  data,
  response = "response",
  score = "human1",
  by = NULL,
  ngrams = 1:2,
  length = FALSE,
  min_docs = 3,
  lambda = NULL,
  folds = 5,
  seed = 1
)

# S3 method for class 'mv_scorer'
tidy(x, ...)

Arguments

data

a data frame with one row per human-scored response.

response, score

names of the columns that hold the response text and the human score used for training.

by

optional name of a column (such as the prompt or item) to train a separate scorer for each of its values.

ngrams

1 for single words, 1:2 to add two-word phrases.

length

logical; add the log number of words as a feature.

min_docs

smallest number of training responses a word must appear in to be used.

lambda

the ridge penalty; NULL chooses it by cross-validation.

folds

number of cross-validation folds.

seed

random seed for the fold split, or NULL.

x

a scorer from train_scorer().

...

not used.

Value

An object of class mv_scorer: A list with one model per value of by (models), the settings, and cv, a tibble of out-of-fold predictions for the training responses (row, by, human, predicted, machine). Use predict() to score new responses, tidy() for the word weights, and agreement_report() to check it.

tidy() returns a tibble with one row per feature and model: by, term and weight, the change in the predicted score for one more use of the word (on the log(1 + count) scale), sorted from the largest positive weight.

Details

Each response is turned into counts of its words and, with ngrams = 1:2, of its two-word phrases, kept when they appear in at least min_docs training responses. The counts enter as log(1 + count). With length = TRUE the log of the number of words is added as a feature, as many commercial engines do. The ridge penalty lambda is chosen by folds-fold cross-validation unless you give it, and the cross-validated predictions are kept, so the scorer's agreement with people can be judged on responses it was not trained on (see agreement_report()).

A ridge regression treats scoring as prediction: It learns which words go with high human scores in the training responses, whatever the reason. Words that signal a key idea help, but so can words that merely go with longer or more fluent answers. That is why the scorer's agreement must be checked overall and within groups before its scores are used.

See also

score_open() to use the scorer in an assessment pipeline, agreement_report() to check it; the AI Hub.

Examples

e1 <- essays[essays$prompt == "E1", ]
s <- train_scorer(e1, response = "response", score = "human1")
s
#> <mv_scorer> ridge regression on words and two-word phrases
#>   400 responses, 662 features, lambda = 10, cross-validated RMSE = 0.56, QWK = 0.89
#> Check it with agreement_report(); use it with predict() or score_open().
head(tidy(s))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   by    term    weight
#>   <chr> <chr>    <dbl>
#> 1 all   less     0.425
#> 2 all   with     0.347
#> 3 all   is less  0.314
#> 4 all   than     0.281
#> 5 all   on       0.249
#> 6 all   are      0.244
predict(s, c("Ice is less dense than water, so it floats.", "I don't know."))
#> [1] 1 0
